statement: If in an equilateral and equiangular pentagon straight lines subtend two angles taken in order, they cut one another in extreme and mean ratio, and their greater segments are equal to the side of the pentagon.
heath_proof: For in the equilateral and equiangular pentagon ABCDE let the straight lines AC, BE, cutting one another at the point H, subtend two angles taken in order, the angles at A, B; I say that each of them has been cut in extreme and mean ratio at the point H, and their greater segments are equal to the side of the pentagon. For let the circle ABCDE be circumscribed about the pentagon ABCDE. [IV. 14] Then, since the two straight lines EA, AB are equal to the two AB, BC, and they contain equal angles, therefore the base BE is equal to the base AC, the triangle ABE is equal to the triangle ABC, and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining angles respectively, namely those which the equal sides subtend. [I. 4] Therefore the angle BAC is equal to the angle ABE; therefore the angle AHE is double of the angle BAH. [I. 32] But the angle EAC is also double of the angle BAC, inasmuch as the circumference EDC is also double of the circumference CB; [III. 28, VI. 33] therefore the angle HAE is equal to the angle AHE; hence the straight line HE is also equal to EA, that is, to AB. [I. 6] And, since the straight line BA is equal to AE, the angle ABE is also equal to the angle AEB. [I. 5] But the angle ABE was proved equal to the angle BAH; therefore the angle BEA is also equal to the angle BAH. And the angle ABE is common to the two triangles ABE and ABH; therefore the remaining angle BAE is equal to the remaining angle AHB; [I. 32] therefore the triangle ABE is equiangular with the triangle ABH; therefore, proportionally, as EB is to BA, so is AB to BH. [VI. 4] But BA is equal to EH; therefore, as BE is to EH, so is EH to HB. And BE is greater than EH; therefore EH is also greater than HB. [V. 14] Therefore BE has been cut in extreme and mean ratio at H, and the greater segment HE is equal to the side of the pentagon. Similarly we can prove that AC has also been cut in extreme and mean ratio at H, and its greater segment CH is equal to the side of the pentagon.
ai_proof_text:
13.8
**Statement:** If in an equilateral and equiangular pentagon straight lines subtend two angles taken in order, they cut one another in extreme and mean ratio, and their greater segments are equal to the side of the pentagon.

**Step 1.** Let ABCDE be the equilateral and equiangular pentagon. Join AC and BE [P1]; AC subtends the angle ABC and BE subtends the angle BAE, two angles of the pentagon taken in order. Let AC and BE cut one another at H, so that H lies between B and E on BE and between A and C on AC. It is to be proved that BE and AC are each cut at H in extreme and mean ratio, and that their greater segments are equal to the side of the pentagon.

**Step 2.** In the triangles EAB and ABC, EA = AB and AB = BC, since the pentagon is equilateral, and the angle EAB = the angle ABC, since the pentagon is equiangular. Therefore the base EB = the base AC, and the remaining angles are equal to the remaining angles which the equal sides subtend: the angle AEB = the angle BAC, and the angle ABE = the angle BCA [1.4].

**Step 3.** In the triangle EAB, since EA = AB, the angle AEB = the angle ABE [1.5]. Combining with Step 2, the angle ABE = the angle AEB = the angle BAC [CN1]. Since H lies on BE and on AC, this says that the angle HBA = the angle HAB.

**Step 4.** In the triangle ABH the side BH is produced to E; hence the exterior angle AHE is equal to the two interior and opposite angles HAB and HBA taken together [1.32]. By Step 3 each of these is equal to the angle BAC, so the angle AHE is equal to the sum of two angles each equal to the angle BAC [CN2].

**Step 5.** Circumscribe the circle ABCDE about the pentagon [4.14]. Since the straight lines AB, BC, CD, DE, EA fitted into this circle are equal, they cut off equal circumferences AB, BC, CD, DE, EA [3.28].

**Step 6.** Join AD [P1]. The angles BAC, CAD, DAE at the circumference stand respectively on the equal circumferences BC, CD, DE; therefore the angle BAC = the angle CAD = the angle DAE [3.27]. Since D lies on the circumference CDE, the straight line AD falls within the angle CAE, so that the angle CAE is the sum of the angles CAD and DAE, that is, the sum of two angles each equal to the angle BAC [CN2]. Hence, by Step 4, the angle HAE (which is the angle CAE) is equal to the angle AHE [CN1].

**Step 7.** In the triangle AHE the angle AHE = the angle HAE; therefore the sides subtending these equal angles are equal, namely EA = EH [1.6]. But EA = AB, being a side of the pentagon; therefore EH = AB, the side of the pentagon [CN1].

**Step 8.** Consider the triangles EBA and ABH. The angle EBA is common to both, since the angle ABH is the same angle. The angle BEA = the angle BAC (Step 2) = the angle BAH, since H lies on AC. Therefore the remaining angle BAE of the triangle EBA is equal to the remaining angle BHA of the triangle ABH, each being what remains when two equal sums are taken from two right angles [1.32, CN3]. The triangles EBA and ABH are therefore equiangular, and the sides about the equal angles are proportional, the corresponding sides being those which subtend the equal angles: as EB is to BA, so is AB to BH [6.4] (EB and AB subtend the equal angles BAE, BHA; BA and BH subtend the equal angles BEA, BAH).

**Step 9.** Since BA = EH (Step 7), EB has to BA the same ratio as EB has to EH, and AB has to BH the same ratio as EH has to HB [5.7]. Therefore, as EB is to EH, so is EH to HB [5.11].

**Step 10.** EB is greater than its part EH [CN5]. In the proportion EB : EH = EH : HB the first magnitude EB is greater than the third EH; therefore the second EH is greater than the fourth HB [5.14]. Thus the whole BE is to its greater segment EH as EH is to the lesser segment HB; that is, BE has been cut in extreme and mean ratio at H [D6.3], and its greater segment EH is equal to the side of the pentagon (Step 7).

**Step 11.** Now for AC. In the triangle ABH the angle HAB = the angle HBA (Step 3); therefore HA = HB [1.6]. Also AC = EB (Step 2). Subtracting the equals HA, HB from the equals AC, EB, the remainders are equal: HC = HE [CN3]. Hence HC = HE = AB, the side of the pentagon [CN1].

**Step 12.** Since AC = EB and HC = EH, AC has to HC the same ratio as EB has to HC, and EB has to HC the same ratio as EB has to EH [5.7]; therefore AC : HC = EB : EH [5.11]. Likewise, since EH = HC and HB = HA, EH : HB = HC : HA [5.7, 5.11]. But EB : EH = EH : HB (Step 9); therefore AC : HC = HC : HA [5.11]. AC is greater than its part HC [CN5], so HC is greater than HA [5.14]. Therefore AC has been cut in extreme and mean ratio at H [D6.3], and its greater segment HC is equal to the side of the pentagon (Step 11).

**Step 13.** Therefore the straight lines AC, BE, which subtend two angles of the equilateral and equiangular pentagon taken in order, cut one another at H in extreme and mean ratio, and their greater segments EH, HC are each equal to the side of the pentagon. Q.E.D.

Path note: the doubling of the angle BAC in Step 6 could alternatively be obtained from the proportionality of angles at the circumference to the arcs they stand on, without joining AD; the equal-arc route was chosen as the more elementary.
